content: Thioacetazone, also known by various names such as thiocetazone, thiacetazone, thiosemicarbazone, benzothiozane, or amithiozone (USAN), is abbreviated as T. This medication is utilized in the treatment of tuberculosis (TB). However, it exhibits only weak activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is primarily effective in preventing the development of resistance to more potent anti-TB drugs, such as isoniazid and rifampicin. Thioacetazone is never used as a standalone treatment for tuberculosis. Instead, it is employed in a manner similar to ethambutol, as part of combination therapy. Notably, thioacetazone is the only anti-TB drug that is ineffective when administered intermittently. There is no therapeutic benefit to including thioacetazone in a treatment regimen that already contains ethambutol. Despite this, many countries in sub-Saharan Africa continue to use thioacetazone due to its extremely low cost. However, its use is steadily declining because it has been associated with severe, and sometimes fatal, skin reactions, particularly in patients who are HIV-positive.
